lessons.title: Lesson 1: Biomechanics in plain words
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain five basic biomechanics terms using an example from your sport.
This lesson builds toward: Given a movement from your own sport, you will explain basic biomechanics terms such as the kinetic chain, range of motion and center of mass, using a correct example for each term.
Biomechanics looks at how forces and body positions create movement. Coaches use it to make technique more efficient and to reduce injury risk.
Five useful words: Joint angle (the angle at a knee, hip or elbow). Range of motion (how far a joint moves). Center of mass (the balance point of your body). Kinetic chain (how force passes from the ground through legs, hips, trunk and arms). Ground reaction force (the push the ground gives back when you push into it).
Example: in a jump shot, force starts in your legs, passes through your hips and trunk, and finishes through your arm and wrist. That is the kinetic chain. An AI assistant can explain any term with an example from your sport.
Words to know:
- Biomechanics: the study of how forces and body positions create movement.
- Kinetic chain: the way force passes from one body part to the next, like legs to hips to arms.
- Center of mass: your body's balance point.
Try it now: Pick one movement from your sport. Ask an AI assistant to explain the kinetic chain in it in simple words. Write it in your own words in three sentences.
You can now explain basic biomechanics terms with an example from your sport.

check.q: What does range of motion describe?
check.why: Range of motion is how far a joint can move.

check.q: You want to explain the kinetic chain in your jump shot. What would you describe?
options: How force passes from the legs up through the body to the ball
check.why: The kinetic chain is how force passes from one body part to the next.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Filming a movement for analysis
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Film a movement from the right angles so it can be analyzed.
This lesson builds toward: Using a phone at practice, you will film a movement from the side and the front with marked camera spots and slow motion, with at least three reps per view and permission from anyone filmed.
Analysis needs good video. Film from the side (to see joint angles front-to-back) and from the front or back (to see knees caving in, hips dropping or arms crossing). Keep the camera at about hip height, steady, and far enough away to see the whole body.
Use your phone's slow-motion mode and good light. Wear clothes that show your body shape, and add tape marks on the floor so you can film from the same spot next time.
Film several repetitions, not just one, and film when you are warmed up. Get permission before filming others, and follow your team's rules.
Step by step:
- Set the phone at hip height on a tripod or stand.
- Film from the side.
- Film from the front or back.
- Use slow motion and good light.
- Mark the camera and athlete spots for next time.
- Film three to five reps.
Words to know:
- Sagittal view: a side view, showing forward-and-back motion.
- Frontal view: a front or back view, showing side-to-side motion.
Try it now: Film one movement from the side and the front, three reps each, with your phone at hip height and slow motion on. Mark the spots.
You can now film a movement properly for biomechanics analysis.

check.q: What does a side view show best?
check.why: A side view shows forward-and-back motion and joint angles clearly.

check.q: You want to film a teammate's sprint start. What do you do first?
options: Use the zoom from far away
check.why: Always get permission before filming other people.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Breaking a skill into phases
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Break your movement into phases and find the key positions.
This lesson builds toward: Given your filmed movement, you will break the skill into phases and capture a labeled key frame for each phase, with the phases confirmed by your coach.
Most sports skills have phases. A throw: wind-up, stride, arm cocking, acceleration, release, follow-through. A sprint start: set, push-off, drive, transition. A jump: approach, plant, take-off, flight, landing.
For each phase, there are key positions coaches look at: where the foot lands, the knee angle at take-off, the trunk angle at release. Your coach can tell you which ones matter most for you.
Use frame-by-frame review in your phone's video app or a free video tool. Pause on the key frame for each phase and take a screenshot. Ask an AI assistant to list the typical phases of your skill, then confirm them with your coach.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for the typical phases of your skill.
- Confirm the phases with your coach.
- Scrub frame by frame through your video.
- Screenshot the key frame for each phase.
- Label each screenshot.
Words to know:
- Phase: one part of a movement, like the wind-up or release.
- Key position: an important body position at a certain moment.
- Frame by frame: stepping through a video one picture at a time.
Try it now: Break your filmed movement into phases. Screenshot and label one key frame for each phase.
You can now break a skill into phases and capture its key positions.

options: A single picture that shows an important position in a phase
The first second of any video
check.why: A key frame captures the key position of a phase.

check.q: AI suggests four phases for your throw. What do you do next?
check.why: Your coach confirms the phases and key positions for your sport.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: AI tools and real change

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Pose estimation: AI that finds your joints
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain what pose estimation does and its limits.
This lesson builds toward: Given a pose-estimation tool or its output, you will explain what pose estimation shows and name what can make it wrong, treating its angles as estimates, not lab measurements.
Pose estimation is AI that finds body points, like shoulders, elbows, hips, knees and ankles, in a photo or video and connects them into a stick figure. Some apps then estimate joint angles.
These tools are useful for seeing positions and comparing reps, but they make mistakes: loose clothing, fast motion, blur, poor light, other people in the frame or a body part hidden behind another can throw them off. Angles from a 2D phone video are estimates, not lab measurements.
If you try a pose app, check its privacy policy, because video of your body is personal data. For minors, a parent should approve. Always check the stick figure against the real video before trusting a number.
Step by step:
- Choose a well-lit, clear clip.
- If you use a pose app, check its privacy policy first.
- Run the clip and look at the stick figure.
- Check it matches the real body in each key frame.
- Treat angles as estimates.
Words to know:
- Pose estimation: AI that finds body points in video and draws a stick figure.
- 2D video: flat video from one camera; it can't measure depth perfectly.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to explain how pose estimation works and three ways it can be wrong. Then look at your key frames and write where a pose tool might struggle.
You can now explain what pose estimation does and why its numbers need checking.

check.q: What does a pose-estimation tool draw on a video?
options: A stick figure on the body's joints
check.why: Pose estimation finds body points and joins them as a stick figure.

check.q: A pose app says your knee angle is 143 degrees in a blurry clip. What do you do?
options: Share it as a lab result
Treat it as an estimate and check the frame yourself
check.why: Blur and one-phone video make angles estimates, not measurements.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Describing one technique point
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Describe one technique point clearly using your screenshots.
This lesson builds toward: Given your key frames, you will describe one technique point in neutral words with screenshots and turn it into a question for your coach, working on only one point at a time.
Pick one thing to look at, not ten. For example: "At take-off, my knee bends much less on my left leg than my right." or "At release, my elbow is below my shoulder."
Describe it with evidence: the phase, the screenshot, and what you see compared with another rep or with a model your coach gives you. An AI assistant can help you write a clear, neutral description: "Help me describe what I see in these two key frames in plain, neutral words." Do not ask it for a diagnosis or a fix for pain.
Bring it to your coach as a question: "I noticed this. Is it something we should work on? What cue should I use?"
Step by step:
- Choose one technique point.
- Pick the screenshots that show it.
- Write a neutral description with the phase.
- Ask your coach if it matters and what cue to use.
Words to know:
- Cue: a short instruction that helps you change a movement, like "tall chest".
- Neutral description: describing what you see without judging or diagnosing.
Try it now: Write one technique point in two neutral sentences with the phase and screenshots. Use AI to make it clearer, then take it to your coach.
You can now describe one technique point with evidence and turn it into a question for your coach.

check.q: What is a neutral description of technique?
options: Saying what you see without diagnosing it
check.why: A neutral description reports what is visible and leaves diagnosis out.

check.q: You see three things you want to fix. What do you take to your coach?
options: One point with its phase and screenshots
A new training plan from AI
check.why: Working on one technique point at a time makes change clearer.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Before and after: did it change?
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Make a side-by-side comparison to see whether technique changed.
This lesson builds toward: After practicing a coach's cue for about two weeks, you will build a side-by-side before-and-after comparison filmed the same way, stopping and getting help if the change causes pain.
After practicing your coach's cue for a few weeks, film again from the same marked spots, same angles, same lighting. Put the before and after key frames side by side in a slide or Canva layout.
Look at the same key position in each. Is the change there? Is it there on every rep or only some? Change takes many repetitions; small progress is still progress.
If a change causes pain, or a movement hurts, stop and tell your athletic trainer, physical therapist or doctor. Technique work should never push through pain.
Step by step:
- Film again from the same spots and angles.
- Pick the same key frames.
- Put before and after side by side.
- Note what changed and on how many reps.
- Review with your coach; report any pain.
Words to know:
- Side-by-side: two images or videos placed next to each other to compare.
- Physical therapist: a licensed professional who helps people recover movement after injury.
Try it now: Final task: practice your coach's cue, film again in two weeks from the same spots, and build a side-by-side before-and-after comparison to review with your coach.
You can now compare before-and-after technique fairly and know when to stop for pain.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Filming One view only, or the camera moved or was too high or low. Side and front views at hip height from marked spots, three reps each. Also notes the spots, slow-motion setting and light so anyone can repeat it. Phases and key frames The phases are missing or not labeled. Each phase has a labeled key frame, confirmed with the coach. Key frames from several reps show the same position each time. Technique point Several points at once, or words that diagnose or judge. One point in two neutral sentences with its phase and screenshots. Also turned it into a clear question the coach answered with one cue. Use of tools App numbers treated as exact measurements. Any pose-tool angle is called an estimate and checked against the frame. Can name what in the clip might make the tool wrong. Before and after The second video was filmed differently, or no comparison was made. A side-by-side comparison from the same spots, angles and light. Also writes what changed, what did not, and any pain reported to the right person. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What makes a before-and-after comparison fair?
options: Filming from new angles each time
Filming from the same spots, angles and light
check.why: Only the technique should change between the two videos.

check.q: The new cue starts to hurt your shoulder. What do you do?
options: Stop and tell your athletic trainer, physical therapist or doctor
check.why: Pain is a reason to stop and see a trained professional.
